summary: Discusses ideas from RFC 1016 on source quench. It separates two causes of congestion in a gateway, which it calls "funneling" and "mismatch". The opinions are personal rather than corporate, and the memo is offered to stimulate discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a reply to a traffic-jam idea. It says jams happen for two different reasons, like many cars squeezed into a narrow road or fast cars meeting a slow road.

questions: what are funneling and mismatch in congestion
how to detect different types of congestion
subtitle: Two types of Internet congestion and how to handle them differently.

tldr.problem: Internet gateways experience congestion, and RFC 1016 proposed using Source Quench messages to slow senders, but the RFC does not distinguish between different causes of congestion that may need different solutions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1018 identifies two qualitatively different types of congestion: Funneling (temporary overload when multiple bursts coincide at one point) and Mismatch (sustained congestion when a sender transmits faster than a downstream link can carry). Different sending strategies may be appropriate for each.
tldr.outcome: The RFC suggests that hosts implementing the Source Quench algorithm would achieve better performance if gateways distinguished between these congestion types and sent quench messages accordingly.

facts.label: Detection mechanism
facts.value: Queue length, packet source identity, link speed

today: RFC 1018 is Informational and contributes to the broader discussion of congestion control in the early Internet. Modern congestion control algorithms such as TCP Congestion Avoidance and QUIC employ more sophisticated mechanisms than Source Quench, including end-to-end feedback and loss detection, but the distinction between different congestion types remains relevant to network design.

sections.title: Two Causes of Gateway Congestion
sections.content: RFC 1018 responds to RFC 1016 on Source Quench (SQuID), which proposed using ICMP Source Quench messages to tell sending hosts to slow down when a gateway's queues overflow. The author observes that Internet gateways experience congestion for at least two qualitatively different reasons, each with different characteristics and potentially requiring different control strategies. Understanding the distinction is important for effective congestion management.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gateway gets too much traffic, there are two different things that might be happening.

sections.title: Funneling and Mismatch Congestion
sections.content:
Funneling occurs when multiple independent data streams from different sources converge at a common point, and several bursts happen to arrive simultaneously. This is short-lived, the result of "bad luck" timing, and expected to clear as individual bursts complete. It is best handled by smoothing the transient overload without excessive control action.

Mismatch occurs when a single sender transmits continuously to a destination, but the Internet path includes a link slower than the source or destination. This congestion is caused by one sender's inadequate information about path capacity, is repeatable and predictable, and lasts as long as the transmission continues. It requires immediate feedback to the sender so the host can adjust its behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Funneling is like many cars arriving at the same intersection at the same time by accident. Mismatch is like a fast highway leading to a narrow road.

sections.title: Strategies and Implementation
sections.content: For Funneling, the RFC suggests monitoring queue length is appropriate, since congestion results from multiple senders. For Mismatch, the RFC recommends immediate Source Quench feedback as soon as datagrams with excessively short inter-arrival times begin arriving, so the source host can immediately adjust. The RFC proposes implementation techniques: gateways could detect Mismatch by identifying multiple packets from the same source on a slow output queue, and could use configuration parameters (based on known subnet types like Ethernet at 10 Mbps or ARPANET at 50 Kbps) to determine appropriate inter-arrival time thresholds. The author emphasizes that while these ideas are "half-baked," real engineering would be needed to develop them further.
sections.plainLanguage: If it is funneling, smooth it out. If it is mismatch, tell the fast sender to slow down right away. The gateway can tell which by counting how many packets from the same source are stuck waiting.

references.text: Prue, W. and J. Postel, "Source Quench", RFC 1016, July 1987.
